question: Is it allowed to claim charity as a tax deduction, and does doing so diminish its reward?
answer:
This is a very good question, and it deals with the notion of... So here in America, for those of you that are watching from other countries, the IRS, or the Internal Revenue Service, which is what we pay our taxes to, allows any contribution to a registered charity to diminish your taxes up to a certain percentage. So if you give X amount to a registered charity, you can claim that X amount and you will get Y amount credit, and that Y amount credit will be deducted from your taxes. So instead of paying $1,000 in taxes, you will pay 1,000 minus Y. So it'll reduce. So basically, you give some charity and you also get some tax deduction bonus, which will save you some money. So our brother is asking: is this halal in Islam? And number two, if it is halal, does it diminish the reward of the charity given?

So it's a very good question, and the response is as follows. Let me rephrase the question: can you do a good deed for the sake of a worldly benefit? Can you do a good deed for the sake of a worldly benefit? Because in reality, you're paying a thousand dollars in, let's say, zakat, and you might get, depending on your tax bracket and everything, three hundred, two hundred dollars basically written off of that amount in your final tax amount that you give. So can you give that thousand dollars and intend as well, "Hey, I'm going to get two, three hundred dollars taken off of my taxes," get a double whammy, get a win-win situation?

The response is that in our religion, we thank Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala that you are allowed to do a good deed for the sake of a financial benefit, as long as you have the intention to please Allah. **So the intention to please Allah and the financial benefit is something that is permissible.** What is impermissible is the intention to please Allah and the intention to impress another human being. If you combine those two, this constitutes minor shirk, and the deed shall be rejected.

So if you stand up to pray and your niyyah is for Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, but you are seeing the people around you and you want to impress them that I am praying a good salah, that salah now becomes tainted by showing off, and that will be rejected by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala as a minor shirk. As a minor shirk. So this is something that is completely not allowed. You give charity, you give $1,000 to the orphanage, but you want to impress the people. The names are being announced: "So-and-so has given... Yasir has given $1,000." "Takbir!" And you feel, yes, that's why I wanted to give; I wanted the people to know I gave $1,000. Those people who do that, it will be rejected.

Our Prophet ﷺ said that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says: I am the least of all beings who needs to be associated with anyone, so anyone who associates Me along with another person, I leave the good deed to that other person, and he can give the reward to that person. So Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala does not accept any deed that is done with the intention of pleasing another entity other than Allah.

However, in Allah's mercy, Allah has allowed a good deed that is done with the intention not to please another entity, but to gain financial reward for ourselves. That is a concession given. It's not the default; it is a concession. And there are many, many evidences for this. Of them is the famous hadith of our Prophet ﷺ in which he says that the most important, or the most rightful, salary that anybody can get, the most rightful earnings that you can get, is for teaching somebody the Qur'an. So you pay somebody to teach yourself or your child the Qur'an: the Prophet ﷺ is saying that earning is the most blessed and the most rightful. The most important salary is the Qur'an teacher's.

Now, the Qur'an teacher: is he not doing an action of worship, to teach somebody the Qur'an? Yes. But you see, if we stopped paying Qur'an teachers, who would teach our kids? We thank Allah that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has allowed religious work to be done for a stipend. But the niyyah has to be for Allah, and then also, yes, for the stipend, no problem.

And also, for example, Allah says in the Qur'an that there's no harm upon you for seeking rizq from Allah during the Hajj. So when you go for Hajj, there's no sin on you if you want to do a business as well. Meaning what? In those days, the Hajj was a long journey, as you know, and people would come from all over the world, as they still do, in the days of Hajj. And so it's the ideal place to have a market, a bazaar. And so what they would do is that after the days of Hajj, they would have a massive bazaar in Mina, and you would have merchants from Uzbekistan, and merchants from Morocco, and merchants from Andalus, and merchants from Syria, and merchants from Yemen, all of them trading goods. It's the ideal international marketplace and bazaar. What better time and place to do that? Right after Hajj, you have a whole week or two of bazaars. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says there is no sin on you.

Because here's the point. Suppose you're a merchant. Suppose you're a seller of hides and tans, or you're a honey merchant, and you're going for Hajj. Now you tell me, wouldn't it come to your mind, "Hey, I can take my furs, my skins, my honey, and I can travel all the way to Mecca, and there will be tens of thousands of people from around the world, and I can make some money and charge a higher price, because back home this is a dime a dozen. But over there, I'm the only merchant from Bukhara selling this," for example, right? "I'm the only jewel merchant from Uzbekistan. I'm the only Moroccan sheep or fur merchant." And so he has the intention: I'm going to go for Hajj, and I'm also going to do a business. What is to be done now? Is it allowed to go for Hajj and also do a business? And Allah explicitly says in the Qur'an there is no sin on you if you desire money from Allah during the Hajj. This is in the Qur'an, Surah Baqarah. Look it up yourselves: Surah Baqarah.

So based on this, dear brother, in Islam there is no sin in giving a charitable donation knowing full well that you will declare it with the IRS and you will get a tax deduction, and you will therefore gain some benefit in that regard. **So therefore, there's no sin whatsoever.** And anybody who says otherwise, frankly, is speaking without knowledge, to be gentle here. He's speaking completely without knowledge.

Now, the question arises, and you asked this question: does it diminish the reward of the charity? And the response is that that is dependent upon your intention. If your intention is 100% for that charity that you are doing, and then you declare it and you realize it's a benefit that Allah is giving you, then your reward is 100%. And if your intention is 80-20 or 70-30, well, then the reward will be based upon your intention.

> إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ

So there are people, non-Muslims, who don't believe in the akhirah, who don't believe in a higher power, and they still give charity for tax deduction purposes. Clearly, they will have zero reward, because they had zero intention. Inshallah, a Muslim can never get to that level, but it is possible that a Muslim primarily gives for the tax deduction purposes and, incidentally, for some reward. Therefore, for that person, the rewards will be according to the sincerity that he had. And there are others for whom the tax deduction is incidental. It's not even something that motivates them; it's not there, it doesn't matter. But they realize, if I give, I can declare it at the end of the year, and when the time comes, they just figure it out and they calculate and whatnot. And inshallah ta'ala, they will get 100% of the reward.

The claim or the notion of not deducting from your taxes, thinking Allah shall reward you, that's not technically correct. If you did it for the sake of Allah sincerely, then you shall be rewarded 100%. And to declare it at the end as a tax deduction or whatnot will not diminish the sincerity, as long as you were sincere in the beginning. So I hope that answers your question, and that you do continue to give lots and lots of charity and continue to claim your exemptions from Uncle Sam.
